newsitem.title: USA: ValuJet says execs received no 1996 bonus.
newsitem.headline: ValuJet says execs received no 1996 bonus.

text.p: ValuJet's top executives received no bonuses in 1996, a reflection of the airline's poor financial performance last year, according to a regulatory filing.

"Due to the company's lack of profitabiliy during 1996, no bonuses were paid to the company's executive officers for the year," the Atlanta-based airline said in its annual proxy statement filed Wednesday with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

In 1996, the company lost $41.5 million, or 76 cents a share, on revenues of $219.6 million as a result of the company's forced shutdown after May's Flight 592 crash. That compares with a profit of $67.7 million, or $1.13 a share, on revenues of $367.8 million in 1995.
As a result, the company's chairman, Robert Priddy, received for 1996 a salary of $135,781, no bonus, no stock options and no other annual compensation, the low-cost carrier said.

Under the terms of a 1993 employment agreement, Priddy is to receive an annual salary of $150,000 through 1998, but his 1996 salary was lower because his pay was suspended when the airline was grounded after the Florida Everglades plane crash, in which all 110 people aboard died.
ValuJet President Lewis Jordan entered into a similar employment agreement, which set his pay at the same level.
Under the terms of their employment agreements, Priddy and Jordan are entitled to a bonus of up to 2 percent of the airline's pretax, pre-bonus income.

However, the low-cost carrier's weak performance could continue. The company last month said it expects to report a "significant" loss in the first quarter, but expects to return to profitability by the third quarter.
ValuJet stock was up 3 cents at $7.69 in afternoon trading on Nasdaq.
